title: Posterior Reversible Encephalopathy Syndrome in a Patient with Systemic Lupus Erythematosus/Systemic Sclerosis Overlap Syndrome
case_prompt: A 32-year-old Mestizo Peruvian woman with a 5-year history of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and limited systemic sclerosis overlap was admitted for active proliferative lupus nephritis despite six prior pulses of cyclophosphamide, the last dose 4 months earlier. On admission her vital signs and neurologic examination were normal. Laboratory studies confirmed moderate SLE activity (SLEDAI score 9) with impaired renal function. On hospital day 7, without additional cytotoxic or immunosuppressive therapy, she developed sudden severe global headache, blood pressure 200/100 mmHg, and five episodes of generalized tonic-clonic seizures. A noncontrast brain CT scan demonstrated bilateral hypodense lesions in the subcortical white matter of the frontal and occipital lobes associated with diffuse brain edema.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome was suspected given the acute headaches, seizures, malignant hypertension, and characteristic bilateral posterior edema — “PRES is a clinicoradiologic entity ... characterized by headache, visual disturbances, seizures, altered mental status, and radiological findings secondary to brain edema predominantly in areas supplied by posterior circulation.”  
2. Neurolupus was considered because the patient has active SLE with new neurologic signs — “In lupus patients, PRES must be differentiated from neurolupus ...”  
3. Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy was in the differential due to her immunosuppressed state — “In lupus patients, PRES must be differentiated from ... infections related with immunosuppressive treatments such as progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy ...”  
4. Antiphospholipid-related thrombosis was a possibility given SLE-associated antiphospholipid syndrome — “In lupus patients, PRES must be differentiated from ... thrombotic events due to antiphospholipid syndrome.”  
5. Neoplasia was considered among imaging mimics — “The differential diagnosis of neuroimages includes neoplasia, encephalitis, inflammatory and infectious processes, demyelinating pathology, and cerebrovascular disease.”  
6. Encephalitis was considered based on the imaging pattern — “The differential diagnosis of neuroimages includes neoplasia, encephalitis, inflammatory and infectious processes, demyelinating pathology, and cerebrovascular disease.”  
7. Infectious and inflammatory processes were considered given her immunosuppression — “The differential diagnosis of neuroimages includes neoplasia, encephalitis, inflammatory and infectious processes, demyelinating pathology, and cerebrovascular disease.”  
8. Demyelinating disease was a consideration in the acute setting — “The differential diagnosis of neuroimages includes neoplasia, encephalitis, inflammatory and infectious processes, demyelinating pathology, and cerebrovascular disease.”  
9. Cerebrovascular disease (infarction or hemorrhage) was evaluated given her hypertension and seizures — “The differential diagnosis of neuroimages includes neoplasia, encephalitis, inflammatory and infectious processes, demyelinating pathology, and cerebrovascular disease.”
